courses.title: Competitive Programming Fundamentals
courses.shortDescription: Master time complexity, binary search and problem-solving basics needed for your first contests.

children.text: Start your CP journey
This course builds the core toolkit of every competitive programmer: complexity analysis, efficient implementation and classic problem patterns.
Each lesson pairs a concept with problems drawn from Codeforces and AtCoder so you train exactly the way you'll compete.

courses.title: Modern C++ for Competitive Programming
courses.shortDescription: A portable C++ toolbox: fast I/O, STL containers, bitsets and the templates top competitors ship by default.

children.text: Write less, run fast
Most contestants waste their first contest hour fighting the language. This course removes that friction with a battle-tested C++ setup.
You will learn fast I/O, the difference between each STL container, and the snippet templates that save you minutes in every round.

courses.title: Data Structures for Contest Programming
courses.shortDescription: Master the data structures that win contests: Fenwick trees, segment trees, heaps and DSU.

children.text: The builder's toolbox
Learn to choose and implement the right structure for every constraint: from O(log n) range queries to union-find in graph problems.
Hands-on implementations are written in C++ and Python with time analysis for every operation.

courses.title: String Algorithms: KMP, Z-Function and Trie
courses.shortDescription: Pattern matching, prefix functions and tries that power every text-heavy contest problem.

children.text: Patterns in the haystack
Strings appear in every third contest problem. Learn the linear-time algorithms behind them without drowning in theory.
From the failure function of KMP to Z-lines and trie-based autocomplete, every algorithm is implemented from scratch.

courses.title: Mathematics for Competitive Programming
courses.shortDescription: Number theory, combinatorics and modular arithmetic — the math toolkit behind hard Codeforces and ICPC tasks.

children.text: The hidden half of every problem
When the algorithm is obvious but the math is not, contests are won by contestants who can count and factorize fast.
Cover primes, modular inverses, binomial coefficients and the combinatorial reasoning that appears in hard ratings.

courses.title: Advanced Algorithms and Graph Theory
courses.shortDescription: Take on DP on trees, flows, and advanced graph algorithms used in ICPC-level problems.

children.text: Beyond the basics
Explore the advanced topics that separate national finalists: tree DP, centroid decomposition, flows and matching.

courses.title: Computational Geometry for ICPC
courses.shortDescription: Vectors, line intersections, polygons and convex hulls implemented with the precision tricks contest setters expect.

children.text: Geometry without the guessing
Geometry problems punish sloppy precision. Learn the double-epsilon conventions, orientation tests and hull algorithms that just work.
We implement every primitive from scratch and stress-test them against brute-force simpler versions.

courses.title: Codeforces and ICPC Contest Preparation
courses.shortDescription: A structured blueprint to climb ratings: reading speed, debugging, math tricks and mock-contest strategy.

children.text: Win the contest, not just the problems
Competitive success is about more than algorithms. Learn how to allocate time, pick problem order and avoid the bugs that cost you rating.

courses.title: Zero to Hero: CP Bootcamp
courses.shortDescription: A guided crash course that takes complete beginners from their first submission to pacing themselves in rated contests.

children.text: One track, every day
The fastest way to learn is a fixed daily routine. This bootcamp gives you the exact sequence: judge setup, language basics, practice loops and self-review.
Finish the track and you will have 60+ solved problems and a repeatable weekly schedule.
Read the constraints first
Learn to pick the right algorithm from the constraints: n <= 10^5 usually means O(n log n), while n <= 10 the factorial or bitmask brute force.
We work through real problem statements and estimate whether the intended solution fits the 2-second time limit.
When the answer is monotonic
Many problems hide a decision function that is monotonic. Detect them, then apply the binary search template on the answer domain.
We solve the classic 'aggressive cows' and 'capacity to ship packages' problems step by step.

lessons.title: Fast I/O and Reading Input Like a Pro

children.text: cin is not the problem, the sync is
A single line turns cin/cout into a match for scanf/printf: ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);. We benchmark it against the raw alternatives.
You also learn custom getchar-based readers for the rare 10^7-input problems.

lessons.title: The STL Toolbox: Containers and Algorithms

children.text: Know your container before you need it
Vector, deque, set, map, unordered_* and the priority_queue each trade off in ways that decide whether your solution passes.
We cover lower_bound, next_permutation, sort with custom comparators and bitset tricks.
Connectivity and shortest paths
Implement union-find with path compression, BFS for unweighted shortest paths, and Dijkstra with a priority queue. Compare when each applies.
Decompose the graph
Tarjan's SCC algorithm, Kahn's topological sort and bridge/cut-point detection with a single DFS low-link pass.
A pattern that knows itself
Build the prefix function and scan any text in O(n + m). We prove why the pointer never moves more than n times.
Strings as trees
Insert, search and prefix-count a billion strings with a trie. Extend it to XOR-max queries with a binary trie.
Every integer is a product of primes
Sieve of Eratosthenes, linear sieve, smallest-prime-factor precomputation and fast factorization via SPF.
Counting under a modulus
Fermat's little theorem, modular inverses, precomputed factorials and nCr queries in O(1) after O(n) setup.
Think in states, not steps
Master digit DP, DP on trees and inclusion-exclusion for counting problems. Practice modular arithmetic under a 10^9 + 7 modulus.
The most reused theorem in ICPC
Dinic's algorithm with the max-flow / min-cut theorem. Then reduce bipartite matching and vertex cover to a flow network.
Every polygon is a vector story
Dot and cross products, orientation tests and the epsilon convention that deletes floating point rage from geometry problems.

lessons.title: Convex Hulls and the Graham Scan

children.text: Wrap every point in a tight fence
Sort by polar angle, maintain a stack with the orientation test, and build the hull in O(n log n).
Rating climbs with discipline
Learn how to read problems fast, order your attempts, manage penalties and template your I/O. Then practice with timed mock contests.
Your first submission
Set up a Codeforces and AtCoder account, pick a language and submit a greeting problem. Learn what WA, TLE and RE mean.
Sixty minutes a day beats six hours on Sunday
Structure a repeatable daily loop: warm-up, one hard problem, editorial review, and a weekly retro log to track your rating drift.

blogPosts.title: Mastering Binary Search: The Predicate Pattern
blogPosts.excerpt: Stop memorizing templates. Learn to think in decision functions and binary search will become automatic.

children.text: The predicate pattern
Every binary-search problem is secretly a monotonic predicate. Identify the boundary you are looking for and the template writes itself.
I break down five Codeforces problems that all reduce to the same predicate trick.

blogPosts.title: 10 Data Structures Every Competitive Programmer Needs
blogPosts.excerpt: From arrays to lazy segment trees: the structures that cover 90 percent of contest problems.

children.text: Cover more ground
A small toolbox of structures gives you outsized coverage. Here is the ranked list and the exact scenarios each one dominates.

blogPosts.title: The Blue to Purple Roadmap on Codeforces
blogPosts.excerpt: A realistic training plan: which topics, how many problems per week, and what to review after every contest.

children.text: A plan beats random grinding
Rating growth is a strategy game. Draft your weekly problem mix by rating band and log every contest with a retro note.
Follow the roadmap for 16 weeks and you will see consistent rating gains.

blogPosts.title: Edge Cases That End Contests
blogPosts.excerpt: Empty inputs, 1-based indexing, overflow: the silent killers of otherwise perfect solutions.

children.text: Kill the bug before it kills you
Most failed submissions are edge cases, not algorithm mistakes. Build a checklist and run it on every problem before submitting.
